name: Freya Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Freya. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say here is confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the Fernley Co-op, the main supermarket in our town, and I split my days between the tills and the deli counter. Mornings I'm slicing ham, weighing olives and doing the hot chicken by eleven, then afternoons I'm on till three. I love the deli because people chat while you cut their cheese, and I know half the town's orders by heart. The bit that wears me out is the four o'clock rush when the school mums and the builders all arrive at once and there's only two of us on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's home like, and how are you set for money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Sam, who drives the number 12 bus, in a rented terrace by the station. Between us we get by, but I've got about three weeks of my share in the bank and that's it. There's the Co-op, a small discount place and a petrol station shop, so if I lost this job I'd be commuting to the city for anything similar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit cheekily, because everyone at the Co-op was panicking about robots last year. I'd say the real fight was always pay and hours, not robots. Online I'd share the union's living wage stuff, same as I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, but it doesn't fix the fact that I'm on the lower end of pay for this job. The Co-op already put in four self-checkouts and the manager, Derek, keeps saying the deli might go to pre-packed. So nothing radical, but my bit of the shop is still wobbly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my mix of deli and tills, and keep asking Derek for the supervisor training he promised in spring. I'd use the AI chat thing on my phone, like I did for the landlord letter, to help with my application. And Sam and I would keep putting fifty a month into the holiday jar, which is really an emergency jar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay, with a little knot in my stomach about the deli. It's my favourite part of the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Derek talking about pre-packed. How real is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Real enough that he's measured the counter twice. If the deli goes, I'm back to tills only, and tills only means fewer hours because the self-checkouts take the quiet times. That's maybe forty pounds a week less, which is our food shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if those hours went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, probably, because Sam can get the bus free with his job. Then my Saturday swimming. I'd hate that, it's the only thing I do just for me.

say: The real fight was always **pay and hours**, not the robots everyone feared.
Shop workers deserve a **living wage**, AI or no AI.
think: She is **relieved**, but her pay is still at the **low end** for the job.
The **deli counter** may go pre-packed, which would cut her hours anyway.
do: **Keep** splitting days between the deli and the tills.
**Push** her manager Derek for the promised **supervisor training**.
Keep putting **fifty a month** into the emergency jar with Sam.
feel: Mostly **okay**, with a small **knot** about losing the deli counter.
S0.quote: If the deli goes, I'm back to tills only, and tills only means fewer hours because the self-checkouts take the quiet times.
fieldNote: Her worry sits on the **deli counter**, not on AI as such.
She uses **AI tools** casually for letters and applications.
Sam's **steady bus job** softens the thin savings, keeping her at uneasy.

steps.text: Ask Derek to book the supervisor training he promised in spring
Use the phone AI chat to polish her supervisor application
Keep putting fifty a month into the emergency jar

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, loudly, that if AI saves the Co-op money, some of that should come back to the people on the floor. At work I'd get people talking about it on breaks. Online I'd share stories of shops that cut staff and then the queues got worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the thinking jobs go first, so ordering and the rota and the customer emails at head office. That doesn't touch my deli slicing straight away. But it means the supervisor job I want might shrink, because the computer does the planning bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop waiting for Derek and look at what's growing instead, maybe the click-and-collect picking, since that's people still. I'd use the AI chat more, to get a sense of what courses are worth it. And I'd join the union properly instead of just liking their posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit cross. I did everything right and the ladder I was climbing is getting shorter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd join the union properly. What's stopped you so far?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Laziness, honestly, and the fee. It's about twelve pounds a month, which sounds like nothing until it's that or the bus pass. But if things start shifting, I'd rather be inside the room than reading about it after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the supervisor job shrinks, what do you picture doing in three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe running the online orders for the Co-op, because someone has to check the substitutions and sort the angry phone calls. Or I train as a teaching assistant, which my mum keeps saying. I'd want to see someone I know do it first, though.

say: If AI saves the Co-op money, some of it should go back to **floor staff**.
Cutting staff for software usually means **longer queues** and worse service.
think: The **thinking jobs** like ordering and rotas go first, not her deli slicing.
The **supervisor role** she wanted could shrink because software does the planning.
do: **Move** towards **click-and-collect** picking, where people are still needed.
**Join** the union properly despite the **twelve pound** monthly fee.
Use the **AI chat** to compare which courses are worth doing.
feel: **Uneasy** and **cross** that the ladder she climbed is getting shorter.
S1.quote: I did everything right and the ladder I was climbing is getting shorter.
fieldNote: She clearly sees that **planning work** goes before **hands-on** work.
Her steady style shows: she wants to **see someone else** retrain first.
The **union fee** competes with the bus pass, which shows how tight money is.

steps.text: Ask to move onto the Co-op's click-and-collect picking team
Pay the twelve pound monthly fee and join the shop workers' union
Use the AI chat to compare teaching assistant and retail courses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need a proper safety net, a basic income or something, because no one can prepare in two years. I'd be marching, honestly, if there was a march in Fernley. At work I'd say let's all sign up together so nobody's left on their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think the Co-op keeps people for a few years after 2028 because the robots for hands-on stuff come later, around 2031. So I'd have till then on the deli and the shelves. After that I don't know what a shop even looks like, and Sam's bus will be driving itself too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd start the teaching assistant course at the college on Thursday evenings, because classrooms might hold on longer than shops. I'd stop the swimming and the car to build a bit of cushion. Once it arrived, I'd apply for anything with kids or old people in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly, because it's both of us at once. One job going we could survive, two we couldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Sam's bus could be driving itself. Have you talked to him about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once, and he laughed it off, said they'll need a driver for the drunk lads on a Friday. I think he's wrong but I don't push it. If we both lost work by 2031 we'd have to move in with my mum, and she's got one spare room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three years between the AI and the robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my window, really. The thinking stuff changes in 2028 but my hands-on job holds on till the robots come. If I don't use those three years to get into something with people, I'm stuck.

say: Nobody can prepare in two years, so we need a **basic income** or proper **safety net**.
Staff should **sign up together** so nobody faces it alone.
think: Her hands-on deli and shelf work probably lasts until the **robots in 2031**.
Both her job and Sam's **bus driving** could go at once.
do: **Start** the **teaching assistant** course on Thursday evenings this year.
**Drop** the car and her swimming to build a **cushion**.
**Apply** for jobs with children or elderly people once AGI arrives.
feel: **Scared**, because both household incomes could go **at once**.
S2.quote: One job going we could survive, two we couldn't.
fieldNote: She treats the **three-year gap** before robots as her escape window.
The real fear is **two incomes** failing together, not hers alone.
Moving in with **her mum** is the fallback she names.

steps.text: Start the teaching assistant course at the college on Thursday evenings
Sell the car and stop the Saturday swimming
Join any march for a basic income in Fernley
Apply for school and care jobs once AGI arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, so the government should fund courses now and the Co-op should give people paid time to do them. I'd post about it, and I'd bring it up at the union branch. People in small towns always get help last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think five years is just about enough for me if I start straight away. AGI in 2031 and robots in 2034 means I've got years on the deli. The thing I'd hate is wasting the first two years waiting to see if it's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the teaching assistant course next September, not this one, once I've seen how my friend Kerry gets on with hers. I'd ask the Co-op for fewer late shifts so I can do placements. And I'd push Sam to look at something too, maybe the council's bus depot office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but more in control. Like I can see the bend in the road before I'm on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for Kerry. What would you want to see from her before you jump?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether she actually got a job at the end, and whether she could live on it. Teaching assistants aren't paid much either, so if it's the same money with more stress, why bother. I'd want proof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to make the course possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, again, that's the big one, it's about a hundred and twenty a month with insurance. And takeaways on Fridays, which Sam won't like. I'd keep the swimming, I'd need it more than ever.

say: The government should fund **courses now**, with **paid time** off from the Co-op.
**Small towns** always get help last, and that has to change.
think: Five years is **just enough** for her if she starts promptly.
Her biggest risk is wasting **two years** waiting to see if it's real.
do: **Enrol** in next September's **teaching assistant** course after seeing Kerry's results.
**Ask** the Co-op for fewer **late shifts** so she can do placements.
**Sell** the car to save about **£120 a month**.
feel: **Nervous** but more **in control**, as if she can see the bend coming.
S3.quote: Teaching assistants aren't paid much either, so if it's the same money with more stress, why bother.
fieldNote: Her steady style is clear: she wants **proof** from her friend Kerry before acting.
She worries about pay in the **new job**, not just losing the old one.
Still **alarmed** because she expects the Co-op job to go by 2034.

steps.text: Enrol on next September's teaching assistant course
Sell the car to save about £120 a month
Raise funded retraining for small towns at the union branch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if the government doesn't waste it. Proper apprenticeships, help with rent while you retrain, all that. I'd keep posting about it, because people forget when it's far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably relax too much. Ten years feels long, and I'd be thirty-seven before robots come for the deli in 2039. I could have a whole second career by then if I'm sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd get the supervisor training done, because it's useful now. Then in two or three years I'd start the teaching assistant course once the first lot have finished it. I'd also try to get Sam and me to save properly, a hundred a month, not fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, mostly. A bit lazy-hopeful, which I know isn't the same as a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably relax too much. What would stop you drifting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing it down, honestly, with dates on the fridge. And telling my mum, because she'll ask every Sunday. I'm steady, but I'm not organised unless someone's watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Sam fit into your ten-year plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd need a plan too, because the buses go the same way. I'd like us both to be in jobs with people in them, and maybe to buy a small place before 2039. That last bit is a dream with our wages.

say: Ten years is a **gift** if the government funds **apprenticeships** and rent help.
People **forget** about change when it feels far away.
think: She could build a **second career** by thirty-seven if she's sensible.
She admits she'd probably **relax too much** with that much time.
do: **Finish** the **supervisor training** this year because it's useful now.
**Start** the **teaching assistant** course in two or three years.
**Raise** joint savings with Sam to **a hundred** a month.
feel: **Hopeful**, though she knows lazy hope isn't a **plan**.
S4.quote: I'm steady, but I'm not organised unless someone's watching.
fieldNote: The decade turns fear into **hope**, but she sees the risk of **drifting**.
She plans **dates on the fridge** and her mum's Sunday questions as accountability.
Still anxious because **both jobs** in the household are exposed to robots.

steps.text: Finish the Co-op supervisor training this year
Start the teaching assistant course in two or three years
Save a hundred a month with Sam instead of fifty

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because Sam and I both go at once and there's no time. What would help is paid time to retrain, so I'm not choosing between a course and the rent. And some kind of basic income while people move over.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the customers. Mrs Allen, one of my regulars, comes to my deli counter because I'm the only person she speaks to all week, and no robot will notice when she stops.

headlineQuote: Mrs Allen, one of my regulars, comes to my deli counter because I'm the only person she speaks to all week, and no robot will notice when she stops.
portrait: Freya, 27, splits her days between the **deli counter** and the tills at Fernley Co-op.
She lives with her partner Sam, a **bus driver**, and has about **three weeks** of savings.
She leans left, backs the **union**, and uses AI tools now and then for letters.
She moves first only once she sees **proof**, waiting on her friend Kerry's course results.
Her mood climbs from **uneasy** to **alarmed** because both household jobs face robots.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028**, because her job and Sam's could go at the **same time**.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid time** to retrain, so she isn't choosing between a course and rent.
A **basic income** while people move into new work.
